description: The BRD's MAPS model: three dispositions, seven roadmaps. Each roadmap declares its milestones and the what-if levers its execution naturally delivers, so the future score is projected with the same engine that calculates today's instead of with a hand-written number.

dispositions.name: Tolerate
dispositions.definition: Optimize while preserving. No changes are required, or the application needs modernization that cannot be achieved within the current calendar year.

dispositions.name: Invest
dispositions.definition: Applications with a functional fit to the business, needed to sustain essential objectives. They may require additional capabilities or have technical constraints to resolve by refactoring or reimagining.

dispositions.name: Eliminate
dispositions.definition: The application leaves the portfolio, reducing the application count.

roadmaps.name: Maintain (Patch)
roadmaps.definition: Also called Retain. The investment needed to keep the application current and secure.
roadmaps.leverRationale: Keeping it current and secure is exactly remediating vulnerabilities and upgrading components. It does not touch the architecture.

roadmaps.name: Rehost
roadmaps.definition: The application moves to another hosting or compute service (AKS, ASE or other) without changing its architecture or functionality. There is no recompilation.
roadmaps.leverRationale: The target platform brings observability and stability. With no recompilation, the architecture and the technical debt stay the same.

roadmaps.name: Maintain (Evolve)
roadmaps.definition: New functionality or capabilities added on top of the current application.
roadmaps.leverRationale: Evolving an application you invest in means keeping it healthy: it gets remediated, its debt paid down and it gets instrumented.

milestones.name: Definition of the capabilities to add

roadmaps.name: Refactor
roadmaps.definition: Changes to the code or the architecture that preserve the original functionality. It takes advantage of modern architectural patterns. Unlike rehost, it requires a deeper commitment to the application's structure. It includes the former rearchitect and re-platform dispositions.
roadmaps.leverRationale: Touching the structure is the opportunity to modernize components, expose native APIs and pay down debt. It is the roadmap with the most levers within reach.

milestones.name: Analysis of the current and target architecture
Definition of patterns and service boundaries

roadmaps.name: Reimagine
roadmaps.definition: Also called Replace. Build a new version of the application from scratch with modern frameworks and development tools, or replace the existing application with a new COTS product, often SaaS.
roadmaps.leverRationale: Building from scratch to current standards reaches every lever. It is also the most expensive and longest roadmap: the score ceiling alone does not justify the decision.

roadmaps.name: Retire
roadmaps.definition: Decommission applications that have become obsolete or redundant, or that no longer deliver enough business value.
roadmaps.leverRationale: The application leaves the portfolio. Its score stops existing rather than improving: investing to raise it would mean spending on something about to be switched off.

milestones.name: Confirmation that there is no active use

roadmaps.name: Consolidate
roadmaps.definition: The functionality is still needed and is consolidated into another application.
roadmaps.leverRationale: The application leaves the portfolio and its functionality lives on in another one. The score that matters afterwards is the receiving application's.

parameters._comment: healthyScore uses the floor of the Solid band shown by the interface, so the alert speaks the same language as the rest of the application. automaticPlanTarget: an application without a MAPS roadmap (and not marked Eliminate) gets an automatic plan with the levers that take it to this score; null turns automatic plans off.

coherenceRules.title: Marked to leave the portfolio, but with products in Invest
coherenceRules.detail: The disposition says to retire the application and the product strategy says to invest in its components. One of the two is out of date.

coherenceRules.title: Tolerate with open critical vulnerabilities
coherenceRules.detail: Tolerating is not the same as accepting critical risk. Maintain (Patch) exists precisely for this: the application should be on that roadmap, or the flaws should be remediated.

coherenceRules.title: Critical application outside the DR plan
coherenceRules.detail: It is marked as business-critical but it is not in disaster recovery scope.

coherenceRules.title: Leaving the portfolio with a significant user base
coherenceRules.detail: Retiring or consolidating an application with this many users requires an explicit migration plan before the decommission date is set.

coherenceRules.title: Reimagine on an application that is already healthy
coherenceRules.detail: Rebuilding from scratch is the most expensive and longest path. With a score that is already solid, the decision should be justified by functional need, not by technical debt.

coherenceRules.title: Disposition without an assigned roadmap
coherenceRules.detail: The application has a disposition but no roadmap, so there is no future plan to project.

coherenceRules.title: The roadmap does not match its disposition
coherenceRules.detail: The disposition/roadmap pair is not one of the seven that MAPS defines. The source data is wrong.

coherenceRules.title: Rehost does not fix missing MFA
coherenceRules.detail: Changing hosting does not change authentication. The application has users and does not use multi-factor: that stays the same after the rehost.
